new_statements.rule_in_words: For nouns carrying an initial prefix vowel or syllabic nasal (ë-, ǹ-, ü-, i.e. the noun-class prefixes), the accent does not fall on the prefix but on the following syllable, the first syllable of the stem (the grave accents in the examples mark that syllable). Nyländer gives no rule for unprefixed nouns, verbs or longer words; read as stem-initial (prefix-skipping) accent, which is all the 1814 statement licenses.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the rule is given only for ë-/ǹ-/ü-initial substantives. Elsewhere (p. 2) the apostrophe in forms like fo'h is said to mark a short preceding vowel, not accent.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms of nouns in a missionary grammar of 1814 (Bullom Shore, Sierra Leone). 'Accent' is used in the 19th-century sense (stress); ë and ü in the examples are vowel-quality letters from the author's 13-vowel table (p. 4), the grave accent marks the accented syllable. The modern description (Childs 2011, Ch. 3 'Prosody') could not be opened; its examples as reproduced on Wikipedia carry tone marks, so the current analysis likely treats Mani as tonal and may supersede or reinterpret this accent statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Nyländer 1814 describes the Bullom of the Bullom Shore north of Freetown (Yongroo Pomoh mission), i.e. Northern Bullom = Bullom So [buy] = bull1247, not Sherbro/Southern Bullom (sher1256). Childs 2011 describes the same language under the name Mani/Mmani as spoken in the Samou region of Guinea and adjacent Sierra Leone (Glottolog and hh.bib equate Mani = Bullom So [buy]). Whether the 1814 Sierra Leone variety and the 21st-century Guinean Mani differ in prosody is not documented in anything opened here.

sources.note: Part I 'Of letters and their powers' (pp. 1-5) gives letter values and a 13-vowel table but nothing on accent; the single accent statement is on p. 8 (Ch. II Of Substantives): nouns beginning with the prefix vowels/nasal ë-, ǹ-, ü- have the accent on the second syllable (examples ëbòll, ënàng, ükùnt, ńfo'h, grave accent marking the accented syllable). No general rule for other words, verbs, or secondary stress; 'accent' used in the 1814 sense of stress. Verified against the page image.
